p.title: Crypto-Oligarchy: The Cryptocurrency Lobby in American Politics
p.venue: SSRN 5080344 (Discussion Paper Series: Notes on the 21st Century)

ext.title: Crypto-Oligarchy: The Cryptocurrency Lobby in American Politics
ext.venue: Discussion Paper Series: Notes on the 21st Century (cover page, dated 2 January 2025). The SSRN 5080344 number from the metadata hint does not appear in the text and could not be confirmed from it.
ext.document_type: Discussion paper (single-author conceptual and historical essay, with an abstract and keywords)
ext.coverage: Full extracted text read in one pass, all 620 lines covering pp. 1-21 including the 48-item reference list. Metadata hint corrected: title and author confirmed from the cover; the SSRN number is not in the text. No Paul markup files exist ("(none)"), so paul_markup is empty.
ext.research_question: How has the cryptocurrency lobby, led by the super PAC Fairshake, shaped the 2024 US election and subsequent policy, and does the sector's trajectory from decentralized anarchism through statism to oligarchy mirror Marxian historical materialism? (pp. 4-6, 11)
ext.theory: Marxian historical materialism, applied as a stage model: cryptoanarchism (bands), then statism (city-states), then oligarchy (concentrated capital and power). Also draws on the co-optation of retail "YOLO capitalism" by institutional and oligarchic actors (pp. 11-15).
ext.data: No dataset, sample, unit of analysis, or N. The quantitative content is a handful of press-reported or self-reported figures: Fairshake raised $203 million for the 2024 cycle (p. 7); Fairshake claims 253 pro-crypto candidates supported in 2024 (p. 8); $78 million raised toward the 2026 midterms to date (p. 9); "100,000 crypto millionaires" with no source in the text (p. 14). Sources cited are press and news items (refs 9, 28, 30, 34). Period covered: roughly 2008 to early 2025.
ext.method: Qualitative narrative essay. It combines descriptive reporting of campaign-finance and election events with conceptual argument. No statistical estimation, no coding scheme, no comparison group, and no formal test.
ext.identification: None. The paper makes no causal claim tested by an identification strategy. Its claims that Fairshake "decisively" influenced outcomes (pp. 9-10) are asserted, not estimated.
ext.scope: Population: the US cryptocurrency industry and its federal political activity, mainly the 2024 federal election cycle. Institutions: super PACs (Fairshake, Protect Progress, Defend American Jobs), Congress (a House-passed digital-asset bill, Senate pending), and federal regulators (SEC, CFTC). Era: 2008 to early 2025, with the 2024 election as the focal event. Also comments briefly on non-US jurisdictions (El Salvador, China), without analysis.

key_findings.finding: Fairshake raised a record $203 million for the 2024 cycle, more than other major super PACs including MAGA Inc. and Senate Majority PAC. Described as the largest pro-crypto super PAC; figures are press-sourced (refs 30, 34).
key_findings.location: p. 7, section 'The Crypto Lobby and the 2024 Election'; repeated p. 13 as 'more money than any other super PAC'

key_findings.finding: Fairshake targeted specific Senate races. It backed Republican Bernie Moreno against incumbent Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio, and opposed Democrat Jon Tester in Montana over his stance on digital currencies.
key_findings.numbers: Ohio and Montana, two named races

key_findings.finding: Affiliated PACs Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs ran advertising that often did not mention cryptocurrency, focusing on candidate integrity or economic policy.
Fairshake claims to have supported 253 pro-crypto candidates in 2024, 'a significant number' of whom won. This is a self-reported figure with no win-rate or counterfactual given.
Major donors Coinbase, Ripple Labs and Andreessen Horowitz each contributed tens of millions of dollars. The paper reads this as a strategy of sustained long-term political investment.
key_findings.numbers: 'tens of millions' per named donor (no exact figures given)

key_findings.finding: Fairshake had begun raising for the 2026 midterms.

The paper asserts Fairshake's campaigns against Katie Porter (California Senate primary) and Jamaal Bowman (NY re-election) show it can 'influence electoral outcomes decisively'. No outcome counterfactual or estimate is offered.
The House passed a bill creating a digital-asset regulatory framework, which faces challenges in the Senate. The paper presents this as a sign of pro-crypto legislative clout.

At the oligarchic stage, the sector is dominated by 'whales' and crypto is an asset class for the powerful. 100,000 crypto millionaires are called the primary beneficiaries. The figure is unsourced in the text.
A proposed US strategic cryptocurrency reserve is read as state co-optation of crypto. The reserve is described as under consideration, and no details are given.
Normative conclusion: it is easier to influence the financial system from within than to dismantle it from outside, and the sector is more likely to reinforce existing inequalities than remove them.

measures: Super PAC receipts: $203M (2024 cycle), $78M toward 2026 to date (press-sourced)
Whale concentration: qualitative only, no index or share is measured
limitations: No limitations section; none are stated by the author.
Implied: no original data; the key figures rely on press reports and Fairshake's own claims.
Implied: no causal or counterfactual evidence that Fairshake spending changed election outcomes or policy, yet the text asserts 'decisive' influence (pp. 9-10).
Implied: the argument is normative and theoretical (historical-materialist stage model), so its stage boundaries are asserted, not tested.
Reference-list defects: ref 26 repeats the phrase 'Necroeconomics, and Vault-Tec.'; ref 39 is an untranslated Cyrillic-titled source.
references_of_note: Goldmacher, S. (2024). Crypto Super PAC Targeting Key Senate Races. NYT (ref 30) - press source for Fairshake targeting.
Morningstar (2024), crypto super PAC fundraising vs MAGA Inc. (ref 34) - press source for the $203M comparison.
DL News (2024), crypto money machine into midterms (ref 28) - press source for 2026 preparations.

Sai, Buckley & Fitzgerald/Le Gear (2021). Taxonomy of centralization in public blockchain systems. IP&M 58(4) (ref 41) - the one concentration-measurement source; relevant to network and centralization measures.
Sai, Buckley & Le Gear (2021). Characterizing wealth inequality in cryptocurrencies. Frontiers in Blockchain 4 (ref 42) - wealth-concentration evidence behind the 'whales' claim.
Nadler & Schär (2020). Decentralized finance, centralized ownership? arXiv:2012.09306 (ref 35) - iterative mapping of token-distribution concentration; a possible method source.
Chohan (2023). Cryptocurrencies and parliamentary oversight, CBRI WP (ref 20) - the author's own treatment of the legislative channel; not in the text beyond the reference.

short_quotes.quote: the crypto-oligarchy mirrors the broader historical evolution described by Marxian historical materialism.

rel.summary_md:
Chohan's discussion paper is an essay, not an empirical study. It describes Fairshake, the crypto super PAC network that also includes Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs, and argues that the industry has moved from crypto-anarchism through statism to an 'oligarchic' stage, using a Marxian stage model. Its numbers come from the press or from Fairshake itself: $203M raised for the 2024 cycle (p. 7), 253 supported candidates with no win rate and no counterfactual (p. 8), $78M already raised toward 2026 (p. 9), and an unsourced count of 100,000 crypto millionaires (p. 14). It names targeted races: Moreno over Brown in Ohio, against Tester in Montana, against Porter in a primary and against Bowman. It says these show 'decisive' influence (pp. 9-10) but estimates nothing, and it notes that many of the ads never mentioned crypto (p. 8).

For Paul's systems the paper adds no measurement or method. Its value is descriptive, and it points the same way in three places.

1. **Crypto money flows mostly through super PACs.** It is corporate-treasury money aimed at elections and often spent against candidates, not PAC contributions to candidate committees. That fits Mentat keeping a separate Super PAC channel and a support/oppose field. It also shows that Melange's flip model cannot see this money at all, because its industry money term counts only direct bank and finserv PAC receipts.
2. **The series breaks in 2024.** A new entrant spent at record scale in its first big cycle, which supports the registry decision to decline a crypto forecast for now.
3. **Primary-contest plays exist in practice.** Industry money has been used to contest primaries, the same kind of play the electoral-plays module models.

None of the paper's claims about effects on outcomes can be used as evidence. That applies especially to the competitiveness multiplier, where reciprocity is still not validated.

bearings.paper_claim: Fairshake raised a record $203M for the 2024 cycle, more than MAGA Inc. and Senate Majority PAC, and had already raised $78M toward the 2026 midterms. All figures are press-sourced (refs 30, 34, 28).
bearings.system_side: The refit registry declines crypto for all three model families (pac, control, lobbying). The stated reason is that there is no growth series and no OpenSecrets code. Admitted industries get phase/drift log models with prior-cycle growth.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence covers federal super PAC receipts in 2024 and the start of the 2026 cycle. It is press-reported and gives no per-cycle history before 2022. It supports the decline in one way: a new entrant at record scale in its first big cycle produces a level break that a phase model anchored on prior cycles cannot represent. It does not show what an admitted crypto model should look like. Any future admission would need a break term, or must start its anchor after 2024. Strength is weak to moderate because the figures are not FEC-verified in the paper.

bearings.paper_claim: Crypto's federal electoral spending ran through super PACs (Fairshake, Protect Progress, Defend American Jobs). Their ads often did not mention crypto. Spending targeted named opponents: against Brown in Ohio, against Tester in Montana, against Porter in a primary, and against Bowman. Coinbase, Ripple and a16z each gave 'tens of millions' (no exact figures).
bearings.system_side: The Mentat crypto workbook has a separate 'Super PAC' scope and a 'Corporate' tier. Its downstream rows carry support_oppose. The cash-transfer graph counts only 24G/24K outgoing transfers and states that it never counts independent expenditures again as transfers. The brain records that 89% of beneficiary dollars were oppose, and that the attributed-estimate producer is unbuilt.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence covers federal races, 2024. It is qualitative and consistent with an oppose-heavy, independent-expenditure-dominated crypto channel, so it supports keeping support/oppose apart and never netting them into 'support'. It does not quantify the oppose share. The 89% figure is the system's own, so the paper neither confirms nor denies it. The point about ads that never mention crypto also means the issue topic of an IE cannot be inferred from ad content.

bearings.paper_claim: Most of the crypto industry's 2024 electoral money ($203M at Fairshake) was spent as super PAC independent expenditure for and against candidates, not as PAC contributions to candidate committees.
bearings.system_side: The industry money leg ind0 is the sum of 'banks' and 'finserv' PAC contributions to each member. It is measured against that member's own receipts R, and it does not include independent expenditures or crypto money.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies only where a CU issue sets crypto against CUs, for example on payments or charter competition. The paper gives no CU-specific case. In that situation the competitor money that matters most here would come through outside spending that the flip model cannot observe, so b would understate the opposing pressure. The paper gives no effect size, and nothing here justifies an IE weight. It names the missing channel only.

bearings.paper_claim: Fairshake spent against Katie Porter in the California Senate primary and against Jamaal Bowman's re-election. The paper calls this 'decisive', but no counterfactual is offered.
bearings.system_side: The contest route 'primary' scores a genuine Opponent by the same-party improvement gap and picks the larger of the primary and general gaps. Contest plays convert opponents in spread().
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a real-world instance of an industry PAC making primary-contest plays at the federal level in 2024. It shows the play type exists. It is not evidence that such plays work, because the outcomes are confounded (Bowman and Porter faced other forces, and no comparison group is given). Do not use it to calibrate conversion.

gaps_exposed: Melange's flip and money-response models do not include super PAC independent expenditures. They see only direct PAC contributions to members ('banks' and 'finserv'). For an industry like crypto that spends mainly as outside money, competitor pressure is invisible to the engine.

The model has no deterrence or spillover term. In the paper's account, punishing a visible opponent such as Brown or Tester is a signal to other members. The engine's money terms act only on the member who receives the money.
Mentat keeps the attributed beneficiary estimate unbuilt, so crypto corporate-treasury money routed through super PACs cannot yet be tied to candidate-level support or oppose totals.
Crypto stays declined in the forecast registry. A cycle-phase method has no way to handle a new entrant whose first big cycle is a level break.
flags: The 'decisive influence' claims (pp. 9-10) and the 253 'supported' candidates (p. 8) have no denominator, no window beyond '2024', no win rate and no counterfactual. Do not quote them as effect evidence, and do not cite them as support for the competitiveness multiplier: reciprocity is NOT validated (D-104..D-108).

Every dollar figure is press-reported or self-reported ($203M, $78M) or unsourced (100,000 millionaires). Any reuse must name the source and the window (2024 cycle; 2026 to date as of about Jan 2025) and treat the figures as unverified against FEC.
The paper's 'oligarchy' and influence framing is normative. Do not carry that language onto staffer or revolving-door edges or into graph ranks (D-025).
The paper makes no SNA proposal and no LDA edge use, so it does not trigger the rejected-proposal or D-021 flags.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper, and none of his positions cite it. It sits closest to his margin note on Kim J. 2025, 'I may need to take into account the presence of conflicting industries', and to his wish to map rival-industry champions. The paper confirms that crypto is now a large, separately organized electoral actor. But it shows that actor working through super PAC spending rather than lobbying filings or bill positions, which is a channel his conflicting-industries idea and the Melange money engine do not yet model. The paper is also the kind of confident ROI and influence narrative that Paul's own evidence tests (the sector-growth study, the competitiveness lane) have not borne out, so it should not raise his confidence in money effects.

related.why: Estimates what post-Citizens United political advertising actually does while adjusting for confounding. That is the causal evidence Chohan's 'decisive' super PAC claims lack.
Shows low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending. Crypto's super PAC-led strategy is a case where the electoral channel runs separately from LDA activity.
Bonica's partisan electoral model has donors directing funds to competitive races, which is the framework for Fairshake's targeting of the Ohio and Montana Senate seats.
A cross-industry political spending memo, likely covering the same crypto, bank and fintech spending universe that Mentat's crypto workbook tracks.
Paul's own cross-industry finance and lobbying report. Chohan supplies narrative context for the crypto sector in it.
Field-experimental evidence that contributions buy access, not outcomes. This cuts against Chohan's unestimated claim of decisive electoral influence.
